nameStory: This tiny lichen doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its Latin name Dictyocatenulata alba. The genus name comes from Greek words meaning 'net' and 'little chain,' referring to how its spores are arranged in chain-like patterns under a microscope. The species name 'alba' means white, though you'll see more green than white when you spot it in the wild.
description: Dictyocatenulata alba is a crusty lichen that forms thin, greenish patches on tree bark in humid forests. Think of it as nature's living paint - a partnership between fungi and algae that creates a barely-there coating on bark surfaces. This is one of New England's more obscure lichens, so thin and subtle that it's easily overlooked by casual observers. It's distinguished by unique upright, stem-like structures called synnemata that produce its spores, though these require magnification to see clearly.

idTips.label: Thin greenish coating
idTips.description: Forms an extremely thin, greenish film on bark that feels smooth to the touch and can look almost like a natural stain or discoloration

idTips.label: Bark-dwelling habit
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on tree bark, never on rocks or soil, creating patches that follow the bark's natural texture

idTips.label: Humid forest preference
idTips.description: Most common in moist woodland areas where the air feels noticeably humid and damp against your skin

idTips.label: Subtle appearance
idTips.description: So thin and understated that you might mistake it for natural bark coloration rather than a living organism

idTips.label: Microscopic features
idTips.description: Produces tiny upright structures and chain-arranged spores that require magnification to observe properly

habitat: Look for this lichen on tree bark in humid, shaded forests throughout New England's lower elevations. It thrives in areas where morning dew lingers and the air feels consistently moist, such as stream valleys, north-facing slopes, or dense woodland understories. You're most likely to find it in mixed deciduous-coniferous forests where the canopy creates a naturally humid microclimate.

seasonality.spring: The thin greenish coating becomes more noticeable as spring moisture and humidity levels rise, making it easier to distinguish from bare bark.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid summer months when frequent rain and dense canopy cover maintain the moist conditions it needs to thrive.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but may appear less vibrant as humidity levels drop and deciduous trees shed their moisture-retaining leaves overhead.
seasonality.winter: Persists year-round but can be harder to spot against wet, dark winter bark, though it remains present and living beneath snow.

funFact: This lichen lived a double life in the scientific world - originally described as a simple bark-dwelling fungus in 1967, it wasn't recognized as actually being a lichen (a fungus-algae partnership) until 2004, meaning it fooled scientists for nearly 40 years!
confusionNotes: Its extremely thin, greenish appearance can be easily mistaken for natural bark discoloration, algae growth, or even dirt and weathering. The key difference is that this lichen maintains a consistent, subtle green tinge and smooth texture, while simple algae or staining tends to be more irregular and patchy.
contextualKnowledge: Scientists are still puzzling over this lichen's true identity - recent DNA studies suggest it might actually be an asexual stage of a completely different lichen genus called Thelenella, meaning what we call Dictyocatenulata alba could be the 'teenage phase' of another species entirely.
compareHints: Since Dictyocatenulata alba is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it with other thin, crusty bark lichens like Graphis species, which typically have distinctive black line-like markings, or Arthonia species, which often appear as dark spots rather than greenish films. Unlike these relatives, Dictyocatenulata maintains its subtle greenish color and lacks the bold markings of most other bark lichens.
